title: How Painful Does Success Need to Be?
subtitle: It might be less than advertised.
html:
“I still find myself with this sense that success has to be earned.

And the only way to earn it is to inflict pain on yourself.

And if you’re not in pain, you didn’t try hard enough.

And it would have been better if you’d suffered more.

And I think that’s a lie, and I want to find out if it’s a lie or if it’s true.” — Rich Roll (hopefully)1

Can a 10% reduction in average work rate lead to a 10%, 100%, or 1000% increase in your well-being?

I sure hope so.

It’s natural for the insecure overachiever to work as much as they can—shedding the weight of relationships, hobbies, and community in pursuit of their goals. Doing so makes them light, agile, and able to progress quickly. This kind of hermitage is an effective strategy. After all, when you get rid of everything but the work, the only thing you have left to do is the work. For our purposes, let’s make this our operational definition of working at 100% capacity: working so much that, besides doing the bare essentials—eating, sleeping, pooping, etc.—you do nothing but work. Working at 100% capacity sucks. It feels like it sucks, and it looks like it sucks. It’s inhuman. It just sucks.

Many, though, feel it’s noble to climb toward 100% capacity as if it were an asymptote—finding ways to crawl forever nearer to it so we might one day transcend Work altogether and become Work itself… or something like that. Anything short of constantly striving to do more breeds guilt and shame. “What a worthless clump of cells you are that you only worked a 12-hour day instead of 18. You’re falling behind,” the internal monologue sneers.

Behind what? Behind some fantastical version of yourself that doesn’t abide by the laws of physics? That has no biological drives—for connection, sleep, or... oh, I don’t know… a shower? (I’m talking to you, CS bros)

What are we actually after here?

If we think about it for more than 7 seconds, we realize that the goal of work isn’t to work; it’s to create value, to capture some of that value for yourself (in a salary, commission, etc.), and—if you’re lucky—to enjoy the value-creation process itself. That “value” might be a widget, a cup of coffee, or a well-polished shoe. It doesn’t matter. What matters is that:

  1. we create value,

  2. we capture enough of the value to live life, and

  3. the value-creation process gives us a feeling other than pure misery or anhedonia2. *Insert cliché about it being about the journey, not the destination.

When work metastasizes from hour to hour, until no hour is left untouched, it diminishes our ability to live life, which was one of the principal reasons for working in the first place!

For many of us, The WorkTM calls to us as the Sirens called to Odysseus—but we have no mast to which we can tie ourselves. Society encourages us to be seduced. It rewards winners, and winning requires working hard. Really hard. But he who is miserable is not winning. He who is winning is winning. And victory does not necessarily go to he who burned their candle the fastest. Being able to work harder than everyone doesn’t mean that you should, and failing to resist the gravitational pull of the 100%-capacity asymptote might earn us wealth at the cost of our lives.

But what does life look like at 90%?

At 90%, we can maintain the hold on community, adventure, and play that would have otherwise slipped through our fingers. We can have our health, hobbies, and community. We can start a family, build an empire, or start a family while building an empire. It just might take us 1.11 (= 1 / 0.90) times longer to achieve certain goals. And that’s okay. We have time. We can take a deep breath.

“Life, if lived well, is long enough.” — Seneca

1

I yanked this from Chris Williamson’s newsletter, but I couldn’t find where Rich Roll ever said this.

2

Anhedonia — the inability to feel pleasure or joy from activities you once liked.
